## Introduction

This page covers how the shell finds the programs you run (the `$PATH`),
and how you can make lasting changes to your shell's settings
using configuration files like `~/.bashrc`.
Understanding the `$PATH` helps you make sense of `command not found` errors,
and of which version of a program runs when several are installed.
And with a few lines in your `~/.bashrc`,
you can make your shell more convenient to work in,
e.g. with shortcuts for commands you use often and a more informative prompt.

### Setting up

To run the commands on this page yourself, start a VS Code session at
<https://ondemand.osc.edu> in `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER`.

## `$PATH`: where the shell looks for programs

### What is the `$PATH`?

`$PATH` is an environment variable like `$HOME` and `$USER`,
which you learned about in [week 3](../week03/w3a_shell-basics.qmd).
It contains a list of directories,
and whenever you type the name of a program,
the shell searches these directories for an executable file with that name.
This is why you can run programs without specifying the full path to their executable.

To see where the executable (binary) for a command is located,
you can use the `which` command:

```bash
which git
```
```bash-out
/usr/bin/git
```

To check which directories are in your `$PATH`, you can simply `echo` it:

<!-- TODO: regenerate this output and the numbered one below on Cardinal (current output is from the old Owens/Pitzer setup), then update the line numbers in the callout below -->

```bash
echo $PATH
```
```bash-out
/apps/xalt/xalt/bin:/opt/mvapich2/intel/19.0/2.3.3/bin:/apps/gnu/8.4.0/bin:/opt/intel/19.0.5/itac_latest/bin:/opt/intel/19.0.5/advisor/bin64:/opt/intel/19.0.5/vtune_amplifier/bin64:/opt/intel/19.0.5/inspector_2019/bin64:/opt/intel/19.0.5/compilers_and_libraries_2019/linux/bin/intel64:/apps/software_usage:/usr/lib64/qt-3.3/bin:/opt/osc/bin:/opt/moab/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/sbin:/opt/ibutils/bin:/opt/ddn/ime/bin:/opt/puppetlabs/bin
```

That output is hard to read,
because the directories are separated by colons `:`.
Let's make it a bit more readable by replacing the colons with newlines
(`tr ":" "\n"`), and numbering the lines (`nl`):

```bash
echo $PATH | tr ":" "\n" | nl
```
```bash-out
     1  /apps/xalt/xalt/bin
     2  /opt/mvapich2/intel/19.0/2.3.3/bin
     3  /apps/gnu/8.4.0/bin
     4  /opt/intel/19.0.5/itac_latest/bin
     5  /opt/intel/19.0.5/advisor/bin64
     6  /opt/intel/19.0.5/vtune_amplifier/bin64
     7  /opt/intel/19.0.5/inspector_2019/bin64
     8  /opt/intel/19.0.5/compilers_and_libraries_2019/linux/bin/intel64
     9  /apps/software_usage
    10  /usr/lib64/qt-3.3/bin
    11  /opt/osc/bin
    12  /opt/moab/bin
    13  /usr/local/bin
    14  /usr/bin
    15  /usr/local/sbin
    16  /usr/sbin
    17  /opt/ibutils/bin
    18  /opt/ddn/ime/bin
    19  /opt/puppetlabs/bin
```

The order of the directories matters:
the shell searches them from first to last,
and runs the **first** matching executable that it finds.

::: {.callout-note}
#### Where do the directories in your `$PATH` come from?

You never set any of these directories yourself, so where do they come from?
They were added by different sources when your shell started:

- **Standard Unix directories** like `/usr/bin` and `/usr/local/bin`
  (lines 13–16) are part of the default `$PATH` on any Linux system,
  and contain basic commands like `ls` and `git`.
- **System-wide configuration files** that OSC has set up
  (in `/etc/`, which run for every user when their shell starts)
  add OSC-specific directories like `/opt/osc/bin` (line 11).
- **Modules that OSC loads by default** add the directories at the start
  (lines 1–8), like those for the Intel compilers.
  You can see which modules are currently loaded with `module list`.
- **Your own configuration files** like `~/.bashrc` can add directories as well
  (more on these [below](#shell-configuration-files)).
:::

### Modules (and Conda) change your `$PATH`

In [week 6](../week06/w6b_software.qmd),
you saw that the `fastqc` command is not available until you load its module.
Now you can better understand what `module load` does:
it adds the directory with FastQC's executable to the start of your `$PATH`.

Before loading the module, `which fastqc` shows that the shell cannot find it:

<!-- TODO: regenerate on Cardinal; the $PATH in this output should match the `echo $PATH` output above (no personal micromamba/software/Quarto dirs) -->

```bash
which fastqc
```
```bash-out
/usr/bin/which: no fastqc in (/users/PAS0471/jelmer/micromamba/condabin:/apps/xalt/xalt/bin:/opt/mvapich2/intel/19.0/2.3.3/bin:/apps/gnu/8.4.0/bin:/opt/intel/19.0.5/itac_latest/bin:/opt/intel/19.0.5/advisor/bin64:/opt/intel/19.0.5/vtune_amplifier/bin64:/opt/intel/19.0.5/inspector_2019/bin64:/opt/intel/19.0.5/compilers_and_libraries_2019/linux/bin/intel64:/apps/software_usage:/usr/lib64/qt-3.3/bin:/opt/osc/bin:/opt/moab/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/sbin:/opt/ibutils/bin:/opt/ddn/ime/bin:/opt/puppetlabs/bin:/users/PAS0471/jelmer/software/bin/:/users/PAS0471/jelmer/.local/bin:/users/PAS0471/jelmer/software/quarto/quarto-1.10.15/bin)
```

After loading the module, `which fastqc` shows the path to the executable:

```bash
module load fastqc/0.12.1
which fastqc
```
```bash-out
/apps/spack/0.21/cardinal/linux-rhel9-sapphirerapids/fastqc/gcc/11.3.1/0.12.1-ct5vuye/bin/fastqc
```

(Activating a [Conda environment](conda.qmd) works the same way.)

<details class="details-quiz">
<summary>Say you have your own, older `fastqc` in `~/software/bin`, and your `~/.bashrc` adds that dir to the _start_ of your `$PATH`. If you then run `module load fastqc/0.12.1`, which `fastqc` will run?</summary>

The module's version.
Your `~/.bashrc` added your dir to the start of the `$PATH` when the shell started,
but `module load` runs later and adds its own dir in front of that.
When in doubt, `which fastqc` tells you which one will run.

</details>

### Changing your `$PATH`

You can add a directory to your `$PATH` by assigning a new value to the variable
that consists of the old value (`$PATH`), a colon, and the new directory:

```bash
# Add a dir to the _end_ of the $PATH:
export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/software/bin"

# Or add a dir to the _start_ of the $PATH:
export PATH="$HOME/software/bin:$PATH"
```

Like any variable you set in the shell,
this change only affects your **current shell session**.
To make it permanent, you'll need to add the line to a configuration file
--- see [below](#shell-configuration-files).

::: {.callout-note}
#### Some notes on the above commands

- `export` makes a variable available to programs that you run from your shell.
  `$PATH` is already exported, so `export` is not strictly needed here,
  but it is customary to include it.

- We use `$HOME` rather than `~` because the shell does not expand `~`
  inside double quotes.

- Don't forget the `$PATH` part! If you were to run `PATH="$HOME/software/bin"`,
  the shell would no longer find basic commands like `ls`.
  If this happens, simply open a new terminal to start over.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Running your own scripts like any other command _(Click to expand)_

In [w7a](../week07/w7a_scripts1.qmd), you saw that a script in your working dir
needs to be run as `./script.sh` when you don't use `bash script.sh`.
If you put scripts with execute permissions in a directory that is in your `$PATH`,
you can run them from anywhere just by typing their name, e.g.:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/software/bin
cp scripts/fastqc.sh ~/software/bin
chmod +x ~/software/bin/fastqc.sh
export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/software/bin"

# You can now run the script without specifying its path:
fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz results/fastqc
```

For scripts that belong to a specific research project, though,
it is better to keep them within the project dir and run them from there,
so that the project is self-contained and others can rerun your analysis.
:::

## Shell configuration files

### The `~/.bashrc` file

Your Bash shell is configured by hidden text files in your Home dir,
the most important of which is `~/.bashrc`.
The commands in this file are run every time you start a new shell,
so it is the place to store settings that you want to keep.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### What about `~/.bash_profile`? _(Click to expand)_

Strictly speaking, Bash reads different configuration files
depending on the type of shell:

| File              | Read by                      | Example                                                                           |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `~/.bash_profile` | Login shells                 | The shell you get when you first log in.                                          |
| `~/.bashrc`       | Non-login interactive shells | Shells you start when you're already logged in, e.g. by opening another terminal. |

: {.striped}

To avoid having to deal with this odd distinction,
it is common to put all your settings in `~/.bashrc`,
and to have `~/.bash_profile` run `~/.bashrc`.
At OSC, this is set up by default:

```bash
cat ~/.bash_profile
```
```bash-out
# Get the aliases and functions
if [ -f ~/.bashrc ]; then
        . ~/.bashrc
fi
```

This code checks whether `~/.bashrc` exists (`-f`), and if so, runs it
(`.` is a shorthand for the `source` command, which is explained below).
So, you only need to edit your `~/.bashrc`.
:::

### What to put in your `~/.bashrc`

To see what's currently in your `~/.bashrc`,
use `cat` or open the file in VS Code:

<!-- TODO: check this output against a current student's default ~/.bashrc (the hard-coded PATH= line uses the old Owens/Pitzer dirs, and the ~/.bash_aliases block may not be an OSC default) -->

```bash
cat ~/.bashrc
```
```bash-out
# .bashrc

# Source global definitions
if [ -f /etc/bashrc ]; then
        . /etc/bashrc
fi

if [ -f ~/.bash_aliases ]; then
    . ~/.bash_aliases
fi

# Path
PATH=/apps/xalt/xalt/bin:/opt/mvapich2/intel/19.0/2.3.3/bin:/apps/gnu/8.4.0/bin:/opt/intel/19.0.5/itac_latest/bin:/opt/intel/19.0.5/advisor/bin64:/opt/intel/19.0.5/vtune_amplifier/bin64:/opt/intel/19.0.5/inspector_2019/bin64:/opt/intel/19.0.5/compilers_and_libraries_2019/linux/bin/intel64:/apps/software_usage:/usr/lib64/qt-3.3/bin:/opt/osc/bin:/opt/moab/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/sbin:/opt/ibutils/bin:/opt/ddn/ime/bin:/opt/puppetlabs/bin
```

Some things that you can store in this file:

- Changes to your `$PATH`, like the one in the [previous section](#changing-your-path).
- Other **environment variables**, like the `$APPTAINER_CACHEDIR` variable
  from [week 6](../week06/w6b_software.qmd#the-container-image-cache-storage).
- **Aliases**: your own shortcuts for commands --- see [below](#aliases).
- The **look of your prompt**.

To make a change, open the file in VS Code
(e.g. with `File` > `Open File...` and typing `~/.bashrc`),
and add a line at the end.
For example, to permanently add a directory to your `$PATH`:

```{.bash .file filename="&#126;/.bashrc (excerpt)"}
# Add my own software dir to the $PATH:
export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/software/bin"
```

Changes to your `~/.bashrc` take effect in **new** shells,
because the file is read when the shell starts.
To apply changes you just made to your **current** shell as well, run:

```bash
source ~/.bashrc
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Why use the `source` command? _(Click to expand)_

`~/.bashrc` is really a shell script, so
why not run it with `bash ~/.bashrc` instead of `source ~/.bashrc`?

`bash ~/.bashrc` would run the file in a **new** shell,
and any variables or aliases that it sets would disappear
as soon as that shell exits.
In contrast, `source` runs the commands in your **current** shell,
so that its changes stick.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Adding a line to your `~/.bashrc` with `echo` instead _(Click to expand)_

You can also add a line to your `~/.bashrc` without opening the file,
by appending it with `echo` and `>>`:

```bash
echo 'export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/software/bin"' >> ~/.bashrc
```

Two things to watch out for:

- Use `>>` to append, and not `>`, which would overwrite the entire file!

- Use single quotes: with double quotes,
  the shell would replace `$PATH` with its _current_ value
  before the line is written to the file.
  Single quotes make sure that the line is written exactly as shown,
  so that `$PATH` is expanded each time the file is read instead.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
#### Some precautions when editing your `~/.bashrc` _(Click to expand)_

- Make a backup before making changes:

  ```bash
  cp ~/.bashrc ~/.bashrc_backup
  ```

- A mistake in your `~/.bashrc` can cause errors every time you open a shell.
  If that happens, fix or remove the problematic line,
  or restore your backup.
  If your shell won't even start anymore,
  you can still edit the file through the OnDemand `Files` menu
  (check `Show Dotfiles` to see hidden files).

- Be careful with loading software in your `~/.bashrc`,
  e.g. with `module load` or `conda activate`.
  This can be convenient for software that you use all the time,
  but that software will then be loaded in every shell,
  which can cause conflicts that are hard to track down.
  Also, make sure that your scripts don't _rely_ on this:
  they should still load the software they need themselves,
  so that they also work for others.

- Don't add commands that print output, like `echo`.
  This can break tools that transfer files over SSH,
  like `scp`, `sftp`, and `rsync`.
:::

## Aliases

An alias is a custom shortcut for a command.
Aliases save typing for commands you run often,
especially ones with options you always use,
and can help when you have trouble remembering long or complex commands.

You create one with the `alias` command,
followed by the alias name, an equals sign, and the full command in quotes:

```bash
alias l='ls -lh'
l
```
```bash-out
total 32K
drwxrwx---+ 5 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Oct  1 12:37 GA3
drwxrwx---+ 6 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Sep 14 14:41 garrigos
drwxr-x---+ 3 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Sep 11 15:04 week02
drwxr-x---+ 2 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Sep 11 15:32 week03
drwxrwx---+ 6 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Sep 25 15:20 week04
drwxrwx---+ 4 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Sep 28 15:44 week05
drwxrwx---+ 2 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Sep 30 14:14 week06
drwxrwx---+ 4 jelmer PAS0471 4.0K Oct  1 12:09 week07
```

From now on, typing `l` will run `ls -lh`.

You can also add further options and arguments when you use an alias:

```bash
# Add the alias
alias ae='apptainer exec'

# This will now do the same as `apptainer exec <image> <command>`:
container="oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.12.1--104d26ddd9519960"
ae "$container" fastqc --version
```
```bash-out
INFO:    Downloading oras image
384.0MiB / 384.0MiB [=========================================================================================] 100 % 37.5 MiB/s 0s
INFO:    gocryptfs not found, will not be able to use gocryptfs
FastQC v0.12.1
```

Or:

```{.bash .norun}
# Add the alias
alias gcm='git commit -m'

# This will now do the same as `git commit -m "Add new script"`:
gcm "Add new script"
```

To see all aliases that are currently defined, run `alias` without arguments.
OSC has defined a bunch of aliases for you by default,
mostly related to coloring the output of commands like `ls` and `grep`:

```bash
alias
```
```bash-out
alias egrep='egrep --color=auto'
alias fgrep='fgrep --color=auto'
alias grep='grep --color=auto'
alias l.='ls -d .* --color=auto'
alias ll='ls -l --color=auto'
alias ls='ls --color=auto'
alias mc='. /usr/libexec/mc/mc-wrapper.sh'
alias xzegrep='xzegrep --color=auto'
alias xzfgrep='xzfgrep --color=auto'
alias xzgrep='xzgrep --color=auto'
alias zegrep='zegrep --color=auto'
alias zfgrep='zfgrep --color=auto'
alias zgrep='zgrep --color=auto'
```

As with changes to your `$PATH`,
aliases only last for the current shell session,
unless you add them to your `~/.bashrc`:

```{.bash .file filename="&#126;/.bashrc (excerpt)"}
alias l='ls -lh'
```

<details class="details-quiz">
<summary>You add `alias l='ls -lh'` to your `~/.bashrc` and save the file. Then, in a terminal that was already open, you type `l`. What happens?</summary>

You'll get `bash: l: command not found`
(unless you had already typed the `alias` command in that shell).
The `~/.bashrc` file is only read when a shell starts,
so your already-open shell doesn't know about the new alias.
Run `source ~/.bashrc` or open a new terminal.

</details>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-warning}
#### Don't use aliases in scripts
Aliases are a convenience for working interactively.
They are not available in scripts by default,
and even if they were,
a script that relies on your personal aliases would not work for anyone else.
So, always write out the full commands in scripts.
:::

## Customizing your prompt

The look of your prompt is controlled by the variable `$PS1`.
Let's see what it contains by default at OSC:

```bash
echo "$PS1"
```
```bash-out
[\u@\h \W]\$
```

The backslash codes in there are replaced by the shell each time the prompt is shown.
Here are some useful ones:

| Code | Meaning                                                    |
|------|------------------------------------------------------------|
| `\u` | Your user name                                             |
| `\h` | The name of the node you are on                            |
| `\W` | The name of the working dir (without the rest of its path) |
| `\w` | The full path to the working dir (with `~` for your Home dir) |
| `\t` | The current time                                           |
| `\n` | A new line                                                 |
| `\$` | A `$` sign                                                 |

: {.striped}

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

For example, a potentially useful change is to show the full path to your
working dir, so you always know exactly where you are:

<!-- TODO: the example prompts below use Pitzer node p0362; update to a Cardinal node name (c0xxx) -->

```bash
PS1='[\u@\h \w]\$ '
```
```bash-in-nocolor
[jelmer@p0362 /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer]$
```

With a long path, there won't be much room left for your command on the same line.
You can fix that with `\n`, so you type your commands on the next line:

```bash
PS1='[\u@\h \w]\n\$ '
```
```bash-in-nocolor
[jelmer@p0362 /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer]
$
```

You can also add color,
which makes it easier to spot where the output of one command ends and the next
command starts.
For example, to make everything except the `$` bold and blue:

```bash
PS1='\[\e[1;34m\][\u@\h \w]\[\e[0m\]\n\$ '
```
```{=html}
<pre class="bash-in-nocolor"><code><span style="color: #0057d9; font-weight: bold;">[jelmer@p0362 /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer]</span>
$</code></pre>
```

Here, `\[\e[1;34m\]` switches to bold (`1`) blue (`34`) text,
and `\[\e[0m\]` switches back to the default.
Other color codes include `31` (red), `32` (green), `33` (yellow), and `35` (magenta).
The `\[` and `\]` around each color code tell the shell that these characters
take up no space on screen.
If you leave them out, the prompt still looks fine,
but long commands will wrap onto the next line in strange ways.

Finally, you may not care much about seeing your user name and node name
all the time.
If so, you can leave those out and only show the full path to your working dir.
In the example below, the path is bold and blue (`1;34`),
the `$` is bold and magenta (`1;35`),
and the brackets are left in the default color:

```bash
PS1='[\[\e[1;34m\]\w\[\e[0m\]]\[\e[1;35m\]\$\[\e[0m\] '
```
```{=html}
<pre class="bash-in-nocolor"><code>[<span style="color: #0057d9; font-weight: bold;">/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer</span>]<span style="color: #c000c0; font-weight: bold;">$</span></code></pre>
```

Like aliases, a change to `$PS1` only lasts for the current shell session.
This makes it easy to experiment:
if you don't like the result, just open a new shell.
Once you're happy, add the line to your `~/.bashrc`:

```{.bash .file filename="&#126;/.bashrc (excerpt)"}
PS1='\[\e[1;34m\][\u@\h \w]\[\e[0m\]\n\$ '
```

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Why single quotes? _(Click to expand)_

Inside single quotes, nothing is interpreted by the shell,
so `$PS1` stores exactly what you typed,
and the shell fills it in anew each time the prompt is shown.
This matters for anything that should be updated every time.
For example, the variable `$PWD` contains the path to your working dir:

- With `PS1='$PWD \$ '`, the prompt always shows your current working dir.
- With `PS1="$PWD \$ "`, `$PWD` is replaced by its value right away,
  so the prompt keeps showing the dir you were in when you set it,
  even after you `cd` elsewhere.

(This is also why you should use single quotes when adding a line
to your `~/.bashrc` with `echo`, as shown above.)

The quotes also preserve the space after `\$`,
which separates the prompt from the command you type.
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />
